title: Precipitant, object and the kinds of drug interaction

segs.text: Section thirty three. Drug interactions and the words used to describe them. A drug interaction is an adverse drug response produced by giving a drug together with, or exposing it to, another substance, which modifies the patient's response. The other substance need not be a drug: a food, an herbal product, a chemical, or a habit such as smoking or drinking ethanol. Some interactions are used on purpose to improve a therapeutic outcome, though not often.

Every interaction has two players. The precipitant is the drug, chemical, or food causing the interaction; the object drug is the one affected. Foods, chemicals and herbs are precipitants, not object drugs. These are roles, not fixed properties: valproic acid is the precipitant when it displaces phenytoin from plasma proteins, and the object drug when aspirin displaces it.

Interactions inside the body come in two kinds. A pharmacokinetic interaction changes absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion of the object drug, so drug levels change. A pharmacodynamic interaction alters the effect of the drug, producing an antagonistic, synergistic, or additive effect, so those three words belong under pharmacodynamic. A third kind, the pharmaceutical interaction, is an incompatibility when drugs are mixed, for example when preparing intravenous solutions; it happens outside the body and is a pharmaceutics topic.

Two terms recur. Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared per unit time, by the kidneys, the liver or hemodialysis, and it plays a big role in kinetic interactions. A narrow therapeutic index drug is one where small changes in systemic concentration can lead to significant changes in pharmacodynamic response, so a precipitant that moves the level only a little can make the patient toxic or subtherapeutic. Her examples: phenytoin, digoxin, lithium and warfarin.
